sections.title: What you know
sections.content: You know both sets of endings from the last lesson: *hablara* and *hablase*, *tuviera* and *tuviese*. This lesson is about which one to use.

sections.title: Same meaning
sections.content: *-ra* and *-se* mean exactly the same, and they follow the same rules after *que*, after *si* and after *como si*. Nothing in the grammar changes if you swap one for the other: *Quería que vinieras* and *Quería que vinieses* say the same thing. The difference is how often you meet each one, and where.

sections.title: The same sentence in both forms
rows: I wanted you to help me. (the usual form, in speech and in writing)
The same. (more formal, found mostly in writing)
If I had time, I would go. (the usual form)
The same. (older or more formal style)
I did not think they could come.
The same, in a more formal style.

sections.title: Which one to use
sections.content: In Latin America *-ra* is by far the commoner form, in conversation and in most writing. *-se* is a form you meet more in reading than in speech: in older books, in laws and contracts, and in formal speeches. Both are correct, so you can read either without any change of meaning. When you speak or write, use *-ra*; recognise *-se* when you read it. Choose one form for a whole text and keep to it.

items.spanish: Mi abuelo quería que estudiáramos medicina.
items.english: My grandfather wanted us to study medicine.

items.spanish: El director pidió que los alumnos leyesen el reglamento.
items.english: The director asked the students to read the rules.

items.spanish: Si la ley fuese más clara, habría menos problemas.
items.english: If the law were clearer, there would be fewer problems.

sections.content: You know *quisiera* from B2 Unit 9, with *pudiera* and *debiera*: these polite forms only work with *-ra*, and *quisiese* does not soften a request. So *-ra* and *-se* are interchangeable in most places, but not in those three polite forms.
